channel_name: The Compound and Friends · Josh Brown
video_title: How to Pick Stocks Like Morgan Stanley | TCAF 258
gist: Morgan Stanley Wealth Management's Dan Skelly argues the market is in a durable secular bull (not a 1999-style bubble) because today's AI hyperscaler spenders are net-cash, proven, and serving real enterprise demand, but flags a genuine near-term risk that data-center 'deployment constraints' could cause double-ordering of chips/servers; he also details his 40-50 stock concentrated portfolio process and risk-management rules for cutting cyclical vs. secular losers.

themes.theme: Earnings quality and the tariff/pricing hangover

insights.claim: S&P 500 Q2 2025 earnings grew 28% year-over-year at the index level, but the median company only grew earnings 14% year-over-year, a gap that is underdiscussed relative to the AI infrastructure narrative.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: The median-company growth number shows earnings strength is broader than just AI capex names, supporting a broadening-out thesis beyond the Mag 7.
insights.quote: earnings at the index level did 28% year-over-year growth in the second quarter. Um, if I look at the median company, it was 14% growth, which I don't think gets talked about enough.

insights.claim: The average company likely suffered a 'synthetic tariff-related earnings hangover' in the first half of 2025 and is now seeing a mirror-image synthetic operating-leverage earnings boost 12 months later because companies passed through 60-70% of tariff-driven cost increases into prices and did not roll those price increases back once the tariff issue faded from headlines.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Explains margin expansion outside of AI names as a pricing/mix effect rather than pure productivity, and implies 2026 median-company earnings comps get harder once the pricing benefit laps itself in 2027.
insights.quote: we had a synthetic tariff trade related earnings or economic cloud or hangover in the first half of last year. Emerging out of that right now 12 months later is a equally or proportionate synthetic operating leverage earnings boost for the average company.

insights.claim: A landscaper who raised prices 15-20% after COVID input-cost increases never lowered them back down, illustrating a broader pattern of price stickiness across the economy that is showing up in corporate margins.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Sticky post-shock pricing is a structural tailwind to corporate margins that doesn't require a bull macro call to persist.
insights.quote: What I learned from my landscaper after COVID is when he had to take up price 15 to 20% because of cost... he never took it back.

insights.claim: The US economy is in a 'no hiring, no firing' zone that has persisted for roughly two years, and the AI 'labor apocalypse' and 'SaaS apocalypse' narratives from January 2025 have both been disproven so far — the current effect is AI productivity boosting output from existing headcount, not yet net headcount reduction.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: If true, this pushes out the timeline for AI-driven layoffs but also means the full earnings benefit of AI (actual labor cost reduction) is a 12-24 month forward catalyst still to come.
insights.quote: What is happening at the Fortune 500 level... it's productivity on top of existing labor force... I don't think what's coming through just yet... is labor actually being pulled in terms of additional margin and earnings and that's going to be largely AI driven.

insights.claim: The US economy has structurally paradigm-shifted away from cyclical, goods-heavy activity toward a K-shaped income distribution where the top 10% of earners drive roughly 40% of consumption and are much less sensitive to monthly swings in gas and food prices, which is a key reason recession calls (like the 2022-2023 consensus recession call) keep failing.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Investors should stop using traditional cyclical/goods-based recession indicators and instead track top-decile spending and AI-driven earnings as the dominant macro signal.
insights.quote: we have paradigm shifted away from goods to services, away from a normalized income scale to a hyper K-shaped income scale where the 10% is driving 40% and is less elastic to monthly changes in gas and food prices.

themes.theme: AI capex supercycle: bull case vs. bust risk

insights.claim: Unlike the 2000 telecom/dot-com bust, where fiber-optic buildout was funded by customers that had gone public a week earlier (Pets.com, eToys, CDNow) and then vanished, today's AI/cloud infrastructure serves Amazon's roughly 30 million existing enterprise cloud customers spanning hospitals, insurers, manufacturers and government — real, diversified, already-paying demand rather than speculative new entrants.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: This is the strongest structural argument against an imminent 2000-style bust in AI capex: the buyer base is proven and diversified, not a bubble of unprofitable new IPOs.
insights.quote: The customers today are Amazon buying on behalf of its 30 million cloud customers who represent every sector of the economy, hospitals, insurance companies, manufacturers, government.

insights.claim: The biggest wild card undermining the 'this isn't 1999' argument is that the two largest buyers in the AI compute ecosystem (the leading private AI labs) are not public, not profitable, not transparent, and have not been tested through an economic cycle.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: The credit and demand quality of the entire AI capex chain ultimately rests on unproven, opaque private companies — a real tail risk investors can't fully diligence.
insights.quote: the asterisk is the two biggest players in the ecosystem on the buy side are not public yet... not profitable, not particularly transparent yet because they don't have to be, and not proven through any sort of economic cycle. That's the wild card that takes everything I just said and invalidates it a little bit.

insights.claim: Leading private AI labs' annualized revenue run-rate reportedly grew from roughly $10 billion at the end of 2024 to $60-70 billion by mid-2025, an extraordinary growth rate cited as evidence that AI demand still exceeds supply.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: If accurate, this scale of ARR growth would materially support current infrastructure capex levels and argue against an imminent oversupply/bust scenario.
insights.quote: Some of these companies on the privates were printing $10 billion ARRs end of last year. Now they're last month 60, 70 billion.

insights.claim: The real risk in AI capex today is not insufficient end demand but 'deployment constraints' — companies are ordering servers, chips and electrical/industrial components ahead of 40-50 gigawatts of planned data-center capacity over the next 2-3 years, and if those buildings aren't completed on schedule, there is a real risk of double-ordering across the semis/server supply chain.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Watch data-center construction completion rates, not just chip demand headlines — a construction-timeline miss, not a demand collapse, is the more plausible catalyst for an AI capex air pocket.
insights.quote: you are ordering servers and chips and all these electrical components... ahead of 40 gigawatts, 50 gigawatts of projected data center construction production in the next 2 to 3 years. Are all of those buildings going to get built on time?... Is it a risk today? No. But is a risk a year from now? Could be.

insights.claim: Skelly published a note on June 1, 2025 cautioning on semiconductor momentum specifically on the deployment-constraint/double-ordering thesis, ahead of the semis sector topping locally around June 22, 2025 — a directionally correct call.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated, verifiable call that the semis/AI-infra momentum trade was overextended before the summer 2025 rotation away from those names — useful as a track record data point.
insights.quote: We wrote a note back on June 1st... cautioning the semis momentum and our takeaway was... it's more about deployment constraints.

insights.claim: Even if new data-center construction slows, the chips and servers already installed in existing data centers are not 20-year assets like a factory — GPUs likely have a 3-5 year useful/depreciation life — so hyperscalers must keep buying replacement hardware for existing infrastructure regardless of new-build pace, which is an underappreciated durable revenue stream for Nvidia and Dell.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A slowdown in net-new data center construction would not necessarily crater chip revenue the way a factory-capex slowdown would hit an equipment maker, because replacement demand is recurring.
insights.quote: when you build these data centers, you are embedding guaranteed purchases of servers and chips... it's not a 20-year asset.

insights.claim: Hedge fund clients at Morgan Stanley's prime brokerage (the largest in the industry) have largely not re-added AI capex, semiconductor, and memory-stock exposure after the summer 2025 selloff in those names, instead rotating into Mag 7, select software, and healthcare — a positioning signal Skelly views as healthy rather than complacent.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Depressed re-positioning into the prior leadership group after a drawdown reduces crowding risk and argues the AI trade isn't dangerously over-owned again, unlike a typical late-cycle melt-up.
insights.quote: a lot of our hedge fund clients have not re-added... and a lot of the first half winners in AI capex... Not even close. And where have they rotated? They've rotated a tad to Mag 7... but it's been healthcare.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers remain only in the 'fourth or fifth inning' of enterprise cloud migration even before AI is factored in, meaning AI is supercharging an already long-running secular cloud transition rather than being the entire justification for capex — unlike 2000, when laid fiber-optic capacity had no near-term use case and sat dark for roughly a decade until Amazon-scale demand emerged.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Because cloud migration itself has a long runway independent of AI, 'dark GPU' risk (idle AI capacity) is judged lower than 'dark fiber' risk was in 2000, since idle AI capacity can be redirected to core cloud workloads.
insights.quote: You're not in the ninth inning. You're not in the sixth inning. You're probably in the fourth or fifth inning... do we have dark GPUs the way we had dark fiber? Maybe not as likely.

insights.claim: The fact that Nvidia and Broadcom's stocks stayed flat-to-down even after blowout, beat-and-raise earnings in 2025 is read as a bullish signal for cycle duration, not a bearish one — it suggests the market is pricing these names rationally (law of large numbers) rather than chasing them into a euphoric melt-up that would compress the whole cycle into a shorter, more dangerous timeframe.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A market that doesn't reward every AI beat with a 70% pop reduces bubble/melt-up risk and extends the runway of the secular bull rather than shortening it.
insights.quote: If we don't rocket those two stocks up 70% right after earnings, it gives you more potential upside over time... we don't have to have the rise and fall all take place inside of two weeks.

insights.claim: Today's largest AI capex spenders (the former FANG group, now Mag 7) are overwhelmingly net-cash balance sheets that spent a decade on buybacks rather than growth capex — a fundamentally different starting point than the leveraged telecom equipment makers of 1999 that relied on vendor financing to prop up unproven customers.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet quality of today's capex spenders is a genuine structural difference from 2000 and reduces (but doesn't eliminate) credit-driven bust risk.
insights.quote: don't forget these were all mag 7, formerly FANG... net-cash balance sheets... Fang was capital light. They generated excess cash. They bought back stock.

insights.claim: Circular financing arrangements — such as Nvidia taking equity/leverage stakes in AI lab partners it also sells chips to — echo the vendor-financing pattern seen late in the 1998-2000 telecom cycle, and are a genuine risk factor to monitor via credit spreads rather than dismiss outright, even though Nvidia's CEO frames it as a rational use of the company's line-of-sight into partner growth and net-cash balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Circular financing among AI infrastructure players is a legitimate late-cycle warning sign historically, and credit spreads (not just equity prices) are the tool for monitoring it.
insights.quote: vendor financing was a big issue during the boom bust... this is one uh-oh when the equipment suppliers are giving money to the buyer who's then going to buy their equipment. That's usually closer to an end than a beginning.

insights.claim: Oracle's credit default swap (CDS) spreads widened out in fall 2025 and proved to be a leading indicator/predictor of Oracle's subsequent stock underperformance, illustrating that credit markets are already discriminating between higher- and lower-quality AI-capex balance sheets.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Actionable signal: track CDS spreads on major AI capex names as an early-warning indicator for equity moves, since Oracle CDS reportedly led the stock.
insights.quote: that was go back to the fall of 25. Oracle CDS really was the predictor of Oracle stock in the coming year.

insights.claim: Only Microsoft and Johnson & Johnson remain AAA-rated companies in the market, while Oracle's CDS spreads trade wide — showing meaningful credit-quality dispersion within the group of major AI capex spenders that the market is already pricing correctly rather than treating uniformly.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Investors worried about 'AI capex credit risk' should differentiate by issuer rather than treat all hyperscaler debt as homogeneous risk.
insights.quote: Microsoft and J&J are the only two triple rated, uh, AAA rated names in the market left. Oracle CDS spreads trade at very wide levels.

insights.claim: New investment-grade debt and SPV issuance tied to hyperscalers and Nvidia is projected around $200-320 billion in 2026, a scale large enough that some analysts (referencing a note from a prior guest) argue it is contributing to upward pressure on government bond yields.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick (citing a note)
insights.so_what: AI capex financing is now large enough to be a macro factor affecting broad fixed-income markets, not just a tech-sector story.
insights.quote: hyperscalers and Nvidia new investment grade debt and SPVs. It's 200... $320 billion in 2026.

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley's internet analyst Brian Nowak forecasts 2027 AI capex at roughly $1.5 trillion versus a Street consensus closer to $1.2 trillion, continuing an 18-month pattern where Street capex estimates have consistently proven too low and get revised upward every quarter — Skelly's team calls this 'the quarterly tradition.'
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: A persistent pattern of Street underestimating AI capex is a repeatable signal that upward capex revisions (and the stocks that benefit) may continue to surprise positively into 2027.
insights.quote: his numbers for AI capex in 27 are 1.5 trillion, the street is at like 1.2... the street is still low and that's been... the quarterly tradition. Every quarter you can bank on the numbers going higher.

insights.claim: 2027 could resemble 2023 in market character — a return to concentrated Mag 7/AI-enabler outperformance and a 'bigger is better, quality is back' regime — because the average/median company will struggle to lap the one-time synthetic tariff-driven operating-leverage margin boost that powered 2025-26 median-company earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Sets up a specific, checkable forward call: fade market breadth/small-cap exposure and rotate back toward large-cap AI-enabler quality names heading into 2027 as tariff-driven margin comps get difficult.
insights.quote: 27 could look a lot like 23 where it's a return of more monolithic mag 7 outperformance. I think the average company is going to have trouble comping that synthetic tariff operating leverage.

themes.theme: Market structure, positioning and technical signals

insights.claim: Three-month intra-stock correlation is near its lowest level in almost 40 years, meaning individual stocks are trading far more on idiosyncratic fundamentals than as a single index-driven basket, which the hosts cite as evidence the market is functioning well despite the rise of passive/index investing.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Low correlation supports active stock-picking and sector rotation strategies over broad index timing, and undercuts the 'passive investing is breaking price discovery' narrative.
insights.quote: threemonth intra stock correlations is at basically as low as it's been in almost 40 years. Like each stock is marching to the beat of its own drum.

insights.claim: Companies with more than 1% year-over-year gross margin contraction have suffered materially worse 12-month industry-relative returns, per a chart attributed to strategist Adam Parker — margin misses, not just revenue or EPS misses, are being punished consistently across 2025 earnings season.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick (citing Adam Parker)
insights.so_what: Screen for year-over-year gross-margin trend, not just headline growth, as a leading indicator of relative stock performance risk.
insights.quote: the mean 12-month industry group relative return of companies with year-over-year growth margin contractions of more than 1%... these stocks are getting kicked out of them relative to the index... if your gross margins are missing, you are in big big big trouble.

insights.claim: Broadcom's gross margin fell roughly 200 basis points even as the company reported roughly 90%+ revenue growth and beat-and-raised guidance, and its stock fell about 25% into the print — illustrating that margin direction, not headline growth, is currently driving stock reactions.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Even spectacular top-line AI-driven growth doesn't protect a stock if gross margins are compressing — a concrete, checkable case study for margin-focused stock screening.
insights.quote: Broadcom today, by the way, their gross margins fell 200 basis points. Blowout numbers, yeah, their margins weren't great and the stock was down 25% going to the print.

insights.claim: Median S&P 500 stock short interest as a percentage of market cap has been rising steadily across a 30-year chart, and even the least-shorted decile of stocks (a group including Google, Berkshire Hathaway, Morgan Stanley, General Dynamics, Walmart, Amazon, Wells Fargo, Eli Lilly, Apple and Chevron) is at an all-time-high short interest level of about 1.2%, while the most-shorted decile (including Reddit at ~13%, SMCI, Charter, Trade Desk) sits at about 9.8%, its 70th historical percentile.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly / Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Rising short interest even in blue-chip 'unshortable' names suggests hedging of large concentrated long positions rather than a broad bearish market call, and the most-shorted names skew toward idiosyncratic story stocks rather than a coherent macro theme.
insights.quote: the most shorted, it's 9.8%, which is in the 70th percentile. Reddit, 13%.

insights.claim: Elevated short interest across specific stocks (Reddit, SMCI, Charter, Trade Desk) reflects idiosyncratic company-level issues — Reddit facing a Google search-algorithm change that alters its traffic sourcing, SMCI facing an accounting scandal, Charter facing secular cable decline, Trade Desk facing execution problems — rather than a coherent macro or sector-wide bear thesis.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Investors should decompose aggregate short-interest data into idiosyncratic single-stock stories before drawing a macro conclusion from it.
insights.quote: there's idiosyncratic stories in here... the trade desk has been an abomination in a very good tech sector not representative of anything else... SMCI is accounting scandals... charter is cable... Reddit has the Google algorithm change.

insights.claim: Microsoft's stock rally is attributed by the hosts to the 'public divorce' between Microsoft and Sam Altman/OpenAI and the end of Microsoft's AI exclusivity arrangement — freeing Microsoft to use cheaper open-weight models to meet AI product commitments — rather than to Microsoft merely tempering its capex commentary on the prior earnings call, which had been the initial market read.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Reframes the Microsoft rally as an optionality/cost-structure story (freedom to use cheaper models) rather than a simple capex-discipline story — worth tracking as Microsoft diversifies its model dependence.
insights.quote: I think what people really liked was the public divorce with Sam Altman and the end of exclusivity with Open AI... they might be better off using cheaper open-weight models... that's probably where Microsoft gets its mojo back.

insights.claim: High-yield corporate bond spreads have stayed flat/benign while CCC-rated ('triple-C') spreads have ticked up meaningfully, a notable divergence Skelly attributes largely to composition — energy, materials, industrials and private-equity-backed lower-quality issuers within the CCC bucket, sectors benefiting from AI data-center buildout and Middle East geopolitical tailwinds — rather than to a broad credit-quality deterioration signal.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Don't read the CCC-spread widening as a systemic credit-cycle warning; it's largely explained by sector composition shifts tied to AI infrastructure and energy demand rather than a broad risk-off signal.
insights.quote: high yield corporate spreads haven't budged... but the [CCC] stuff is ticking up in a pretty meaningful way... I feel like this series is diverging... in part because of AI and because of some of the compositional and fundamental changes in the energy sector.

insights.claim: The energy sector structurally changed after the 2015 shale/capex bust: executive compensation shifted from production-growth incentives (which caused commodity-price-driven overproduction cycles) to more balanced capital-return incentives, turning many energy companies into higher-dividend, higher-buyback names rather than boom-bust production cyclicals.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Energy sector behavior in the current cycle should not be modeled on the pre-2015 boom-bust production pattern; capital discipline is now structural, supporting dividend/buyback-oriented energy investment theses.
insights.quote: pre the 2015 shale bust... a lot of executive compensation frameworks were incentivized towards production growth... What changed dramatically post the '15 implosion? A lot of the executive compensation structures today are more balanced in terms of capital return.

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley Wealth Management's flagship equity SMA runs a concentrated 40-50 stock long-only portfolio, a philosophy originated in 1995 under strategist Byron Wien, where roughly 40-45 names are 'core' holdings sized near market weight (about 2% each) and 5-6 positions are high-conviction 'big idea' bets (examples cited: Nvidia a decade ago, Visa, Mastercard, Thermo Fisher) intended to compound and offset average performance over a full cycle.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable portfolio-construction template: hold a diversified core near benchmark weight and concentrate true conviction in a handful of secular 'big idea' positions rather than spreading conviction evenly.
insights.quote: we run 40 to 50 stock portfolios... you want to have the majority of your names... be core holding, plus or minus the market... but I also want to build in maybe five, six positions that are big ideas.

insights.claim: The portfolio targets roughly 2-3% tracking error and 30-40% annual turnover, tailored for tax-sensitive retail/wealth-management clients, and sector tilts are kept deliberately modest (2-4 percentage points over/underweight vs. benchmark) so that bottom-up stock selection, not top-down sector calls, drives the majority of excess return.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Investors managing taxable accounts can use this as a template: cap sector deviation to limit unintended macro bets while letting individual stock conviction do the work.
insights.quote: in a 50 stock context, we've been bottom up focused. So do we make sector calls? Yes. But our sector calls are modest in nature, two to four points over-underweight any given sector.

insights.claim: Risk-management rule: cut cyclical losers faster than secular losers, because cyclical earnings deterioration (cited examples: oil rigs in 2014-2015, banks in 2007-2008) tends to compound and rarely produces a V-shaped recovery, whereas genuine secular winners that sell off on a temporary setback (cited example: Visa and Mastercard falling 30% over six months after the 2010 Durbin Amendment, then becoming 10-baggers) typically do recover.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Actionable heuristic for position sizing/exit decisions: treat cyclical drawdowns as a sell signal and secular drawdowns (absent a broken thesis) as a hold/buy signal.
insights.quote: Cut your cyclical losers faster... because the cyclical momentum almost always begets more cyclical downside momentum... if they're really those big idea secular winners... it can almost always come back.

insights.claim: Government/regulatory risk to a stock is almost always temporary and gets over-discounted by the market (cited examples: the 2010 Durbin Amendment on Visa/Mastercard, and periodic antitrust/attorney-general scrutiny of Live Nation), whereas competitive risk — losing market share or fading brand relevance — is far more often permanent and terminal, even for previously high-quality names (cited examples: Nike, Lululemon).
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: When a stock sells off, distinguish regulatory-driven fear (often a buying opportunity) from competitive/market-share erosion (often a genuine reason to exit), rather than treating all bad headlines the same.
insights.quote: the competitive risk is so vastly different... When companies are losing market share, when a brand is starting to fade in terms of its relevance, that is almost always the death nail of many businesses.

insights.claim: The portfolio does not use a hard stop-loss; sell decisions instead follow a largely binary decision tree combining quantitative/'quantamental' signals with a judgment call on whether the original investment thesis — earnings power and competitive moat — has been temporarily or permanently impaired.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Rigid rules-based stop losses may be too blunt for concentrated, tax-sensitive portfolios; a thesis-impairment framework is offered as the alternative discipline.
insights.quote: having a hard and fast stop-loss in a context of 50 stocks... I think is too rigid... it's also just at the end of the day a decision tree, usually binary.

insights.claim: Even a winning position that has doubled and remains thesis-intact can be trimmed or exited purely for opportunity-cost reasons in a concentrated 50-stock portfolio, because fresh capital would rather go to the 41st-best idea than add to a name that has already re-rated — Palo Alto Networks was exited after roughly a two-year hold once it reached about 70x earnings, the top of its AI-security peer valuation range.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Position sizing in a concentrated portfolio is a relative-value decision, not just a thesis-intact/broken binary — winners can and should be sold on valuation/opportunity-cost grounds alone.
insights.quote: my 40th idea isn't as good as my 41st potential idea. It's friction and opportunity cost in the portfolio... [Palo Alto] got to 70 times... it was a high tracking error winner, so let's take it out.

themes.theme: Individual stock mispricings and sector calls

insights.claim: Skelly believes the market is significantly mispricing highly-regulated, data-centric businesses that were 'priced for obsolescence' during the February-March 2025 AI-disruption scare, specifically naming S&P Global and Nasdaq Inc. as names whose earnings have kept growing mid-teens to high-teens while their valuation multiples have stayed flat or compressed.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable long thesis: regulated data/ratings businesses (SPGI, NDAQ) offer AI-adoption upside without the disruption risk the market priced into them in early 2025.
insights.quote: the idea that data-centric businesses were also being priced for obsolescence and in many instances have not rebounded... I think the market is Uber wrong personally.

insights.claim: Bond-rating agencies like S&P Global structurally benefit from the AI-driven corporate-debt issuance boom because bond investors require regulated third-party credit ratings regardless of how good AI tools become — the ratings business can't be disintermediated by AI the way some feared.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Rising AI-related debt issuance is a direct, structural tailwind for regulated ratings agencies, independent of the eventual winners/losers among AI infrastructure names themselves.
insights.quote: bond investors need ratings. They don't... they're not going to take Claude's word for it... Regulated. It's regulated. They have to be rated.

insights.claim: Nasdaq Inc. stock was roughly flat year-to-date despite continued mid-to-high-teens earnings growth because it got caught up in the same February-March 2025 'data businesses are being disrupted by AI' panic, even though its data/analytics segment (its 'crown jewel') shows strong evidence of AI utilization and its listings/exchange business benefits from a coming wave of IPOs.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: A concrete valuation-gap thesis: earnings growth has decoupled from the stock's multiple due to a misplaced disruption narrative, arguing for re-rating upside as fears fade.
insights.quote: NASDAQ for the year, it might be at highs, but for the year point-to-point is flattish. The earnings continue to grow mid-teens to high-teens. The multiple has stayed rarely flattish.

insights.claim: The software sector went through a wide 'dispersion of outcomes' in 2025 rather than the broadly feared AI-driven obsolescence — Skelly's team called software oversold in mid-February 2025 (right after a new AI coding-agent product launch spooked the sector) and was directionally right, but individual stock outcomes varied enormously, with Microsoft and ServiceNow rebounding strongly while Adobe (exited over a year prior) lagged.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Being directionally right on a sector call (software oversold) doesn't guarantee stock-level alpha — dispersion within the 'right' call can still produce mixed portfolio results, reinforcing the need for individual stock selection on top of sector calls.
insights.quote: I said software is oversold in mid-February... My statement was... I think it's very unlikely [AI labs'] business plan is to put a lot of corporate America out of business... more likely... you're going to see chronic interdependence between AI and software... dispersion of outcomes across the spectrum.

insights.claim: Despite persistent bearish social-media narratives that the bottom-income consumer is collapsing, major card-issuing banks (JPMorgan cited by name) now proactively state in earnings calls, without being asked, that delinquencies are well within historical norms and at historic lows, and that auto loans are being paid off — corroborated anecdotally by full flights, packed movie theaters, and busy malls.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Direct company disclosures contradict the 'consumer is secretly collapsing' narrative that circulates online, and investors should weight bank-reported hard data over anecdote-driven social sentiment.
insights.quote: before anyone asks us, everyone's paying their bills. Delinquencies are well within norms and at historic lows and car loans are being paid off.

insights.claim: Buy-now-pay-later lender Affirm's delinquency rate is around 2.3%, remarkably low despite serving a lower-FICO customer base, cited as further evidence against the narrative that the lower-income consumer is quietly deteriorating.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Even the segment of consumer credit most exposed to lower-FICO borrowers is showing low delinquency, undercutting the bearish bottom-of-K narrative.
insights.quote: The delinquency rate is nowhere. It's nowhere. It's 2.3%.

insights.claim: Official economic data, which traces its methodology back to the 1950s, likely understates real household income and resilience because it doesn't fully capture gig-economy earnings, side-hustle/influencer income, and gambling/betting winnings, all of which accelerated after COVID and continue to grow.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Bearish readings of headline wage/income data may be overstated because the data collection methodology misses a growing share of real household cash flow.
insights.quote: the data come from the 1950s. We didn't have that... on the one hand the data is skewed but on the other hand let's face it, the middle lower income cohort has been more resilient than most have perceived.

insights.claim: New US business formation is running at a two-decade high, which Skelly attributes partly to AI lowering the barriers to entrepreneurship by giving small/new businesses scale in advertising, marketing, and process automation without needing to hire.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: AI-enabled entrepreneurship may be an underappreciated driver of labor-market resilience and consumer income that isn't fully captured in traditional payroll data.
insights.quote: new business formations that are two-decade high is part of that vis-a-vis AI. I absolutely think so. AI in many ways is lowering the barriers to entry to being an entrepreneur.

insights.claim: Roughly 40% of US homes are owned outright with no mortgage, meaning a large, aging cohort of homeowners holds substantial unlevered capital that insulates them from rate-driven housing-affordability stress and supports consumption.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: This stat is a structural underpinning for consumer resilience that isn't sensitive to current mortgage rates and should be weighed against bearish housing-affordability narratives.
insights.quote: something like 40% of homes in the US are owned outright, no mortgage. So think about an aging population with excess capital on hand.

insights.claim: It's a mistake to extrapolate broad consumer-economy conclusions from misses at consumer-staples/QSR companies like McDonald's, Shake Shack, Chipotle, Hershey, and PepsiCo's Frito-Lay division, because those misses are better explained by GLP-1 weight-loss drug demand destruction and idiosyncratic commodity cost spikes (beef, oil, packaging) than by a genuine broad-based consumer downturn.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Don't read weak QSR/snack-food earnings as a macro consumer signal — filter out GLP-1 and commodity-cost noise before drawing conclusions about overall consumer health.
insights.quote: the mistake is to look at McDonald's earnings and try to extrapolate something about the economy cuz it's just not the way... I think the GLP thing is real... Frito-Lay and some of the food businesses missing their organic revenue growth targets for like 2 to 3 years running.

themes.theme: Small caps, demographics and structural labor shifts

insights.claim: Roughly 80% of US companies generating $100 million or more in revenue are now private, meaning the public Russell 2000 index has a negative selection bias, and about 40% of Russell 2000 constituents are unprofitable — retail investors' true 'small cap' exposure increasingly lives in private markets/alts rather than the public small-cap index.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Reassess whether public small-cap index exposure still represents genuine 'small cap America' given the massive shift of quality growth companies into private markets — private/alt allocation may be a more accurate substitute.
insights.quote: something like 80% of the companies in the US today that generate 100 million plus revenue are private... the Russell 2000 which is like whatever the stat is, 40% of that index isn't profitable.

insights.claim: Small caps face a two-sided AI risk: a 'left tail' risk of being disintermediated entirely by AI in commoditizable industries, and a 'right tail' risk of being unable to participate in the AI adoption wave because less-profitable small caps often lack the capital to invest in AI, unlike large caps who can capture AI's benefits.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Small-cap outperformance calls should be treated cautiously and selectively — AI is a structural headwind for the group on both the disruption and the capital-access dimensions.
insights.quote: they might have a left tail risk disintermediation, they may have a right tail risk in terms of not participating in the AI adoption.

insights.claim: Declining birth rates across the US, Europe, China, and South Korea will create structural labor shortages in specific sectors (nursing was specifically flagged) that will likely accelerate demand for robotics, automation, and AI as a structural labor substitute rather than merely a productivity nice-to-have.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Frame robotics/automation investment theses around demographic necessity (labor shortages) rather than purely discretionary cost-cutting, which supports durability of the theme across economic cycles.
insights.quote: Europe, China, the Koreans are not reproducing anymore... we're going to have a nursing shortage here pretty soon. We're going to have shortages of specific careers and it'll only get exacerbated by a slower population growth.

themes.theme: Political catalysts and near-term market path

insights.claim: The politically charged backlash against AI data centers (astroturfed local protests, anti-Microsoft sentiment) is expected to fade quickly once the 2026 midterm election cycle passes, since it functions primarily as a political talking point rather than a durable structural headwind to data-center construction.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Political data-center opposition is likely a transient, election-cycle-linked risk rather than a persistent regulatory drag on AI infrastructure buildout.
insights.quote: these astroturfed data center protests might very quickly go away because there's no longer a political opportunity... then the election comes and goes and nobody's talking about it anymore.

insights.claim: Policy shocks, tariffs, and geopolitical flare-ups (the April 2025 'Liberation Day' tariff announcement, the March/April 2025 Iran conflict) have each mattered for the market for a brief window but the dominant narrative consistently reverts back to earnings and AI — described by Skelly as behaving 'like pop-up ads' that come and go without derailing the underlying trend.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Investors should treat episodic macro/political shocks as tradeable noise rather than as reasons to abandon a strong underlying earnings/AI thesis, given the repeated pattern of quick market recovery.
insights.quote: policy shocks, inflation pressures, all of these factors and dynamics that used to matter more to markets are like pop-up ads today. They kind of come and go and the main narrative keeps coming back to earnings and AI.

insights.claim: AI capex spending could see a 'pull-forward' surge ahead of the 2028 presidential election once the 2026 midterms pass, echoing the Y2K-driven capex pull-forward whose hangover began to be felt in Q2 2000 — a potential negative catalyst/timing risk for the data-center buildout cycle.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly (citing Brian Nowak)
insights.so_what: Watch for accelerated, front-loaded AI capex spending in 2026-2027 as a setup for a subsequent digestion/hangover period, similar to the post-Y2K capex air pocket.
insights.quote: the last capex cycle that became a pull forward was Y2K, and the hangover from that started to be felt in the second quarter of 2000... you have maybe almost a pull forward ahead of 28 in terms of the data center trying to get as much done ahead of that.

insights.claim: Retail wealth-management clients have historically been strong buyers of dips over the past 1, 5, and 15 years and have been the incremental buyer stepping in when index/mutual-fund structural constraints (such position caps preventing funds from going overweight a single name like Nvidia) limit institutional buying power.
insights.speaker: Dan Skelly
insights.so_what: Retail flow, not just institutional positioning, has become a structurally important marginal buyer of dips in mega-cap AI winners — a persistent demand source to factor into drawdown-recovery expectations.
insights.quote: a lot of our wealth clients... have bought the dip. When you look at the trading patterns and the statistics in the last year, 5 years, 15 years, they've been better buyers on the dip and a lot of them have gone back to Nvidia.
